subject: mathematics
question_text: If |a| = 2, |b| = 3, |c| = 4 and each of a, b, c is perpendicular to the sum of the other two vectors, find |a + b + c|.

mark_split.label: Write the three conditions as dot products
Add them to get a·b + b·c + c·a = 0
Substitute and take the square root

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IA (2026-27 edition), chapter 7 PRODUCT OF VECTORS, Short Answer question 7, book p.68. Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. Computed twice. Route one, the route on the page: adding a·(b + c) = 0, b·(c + a) = 0 and c·(a + b) = 0 gives 2(a·b + b·c + c·a) = 0, so the identity |a + b + c|² = |a|² + |b|² + |c|² + 2(a·b + b·c + c·a) leaves 4 + 9 + 16 = 29 and |a + b + c| = √29 ≈ 5.385. Route two, checked separately: a·(b + c) = 0 means a·(a + b + c) = |a|² = 4, and likewise b·(a + b + c) = 9 and c·(a + b + c) = 16; adding those three gives (a + b + c)·(a + b + c) = 29 directly. Both routes give 29. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the Mathematics-IA volume prints no per-step mark allocation on any answer. The 1+1+1+1 split rewards the four separate acts: turning the words into dot-product equations, adding them, expanding the square of the sum, and substituting. Paper position: Maths-1A Section B runs Q11 to Q18 at 4 marks each, answer any 6 of 8, under the 2026-27 pattern; Product of Vectors carries a Section B slot on the paper and also appears in Section C. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

recall_prompt: Say how you would find the length of a + b + c from these conditions — name each move in order.

steps.label: Write the three conditions
steps.margin_note: First mark. Three separate sentences in the question become three separate equations. Each vector is perpendicular to the sum of the OTHER two, so no equation contains a vector dotted with itself.
steps.memory_tip: Perpendicular means dot product zero. Three vectors give three equations, not one.

steps.why: The question gives its information in words. Only after each condition is a dot product equation can the algebra of the scalar product be used on it.
common_mistakes: Writing only one equation instead of all three.
Including the vector itself in its own bracket, for example a·(a + b + c).

steps.label: Add the three conditions
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Every pair appears twice in the sum, once each way round, and the dot product is commutative, so the six terms collapse to twice the three distinct products.
steps.memory_tip: Adding all three conditions makes each pair appear twice, so the total is 2(a·b + b·c + c·a).

recall.must_convey: That adding the three equations gives 2(a·b + b·c + c·a) = 0, so a·b + b·c + c·a = 0.
accept: add the three equations and every pair appears twice
two times a dot b plus b dot c plus c dot a equals zero
the sum of the three pairwise dot products is zero

steps.why: The expansion of |a + b + c|² needs exactly the quantity a·b + b·c + c·a, and adding the three given conditions is the shortest way to show that quantity is zero.
common_mistakes: Jumping from the sum of the three pairwise dot products being zero to each one separately being zero — the addition alone does not give that.
Forgetting the factor 2 when collecting the pairs.

steps.label: Expand the square of the sum
steps.margin_note: Third mark. The square of a sum of three vectors follows the same pattern as ordinary algebra: three squares and twice each of the three cross terms.
steps.memory_tip: Square of a sum of three: three squares plus twice each of the three pairs.

accept: the square of the sum is the sum of the squares plus twice the pairs
expand a plus b plus c dotted with itself
mod a squared plus mod b squared plus mod c squared plus two times the pairs
sum square ante moodu squares plus two times pairs
dot the sum with itself and collect terms

steps.why: The length of a vector is found through its dot product with itself, so the only way to reach |a + b + c| is to expand |a + b + c|² first.
common_mistakes: Writing |a + b + c| = |a| + |b| + |c|, which is false unless all three point the same way.
Dropping the factor 2 in front of the cross terms.

steps.label: Substitute and take the root
steps.margin_note: Last mark. The whole cross-term bracket is zero, so only the three squared lengths survive. 29 is not a perfect square, so leave the answer as √29.
steps.memory_tip: With the cross terms zero, only 2² + 3² + 4² is left.

recall.must_convey: That substituting the given lengths and the zero cross-term gives 29, so |a + b + c| = √29.

steps.why: The condition in the question exists only to make the cross terms zero. Once they are gone the three lengths behave like the sides of a box, and the answer is the length of its long diagonal.
common_mistakes: Giving 29 as the final answer instead of √29.
Writing √29 as 2 + 3 + 4 = 9 by adding the lengths.
